en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 11.
Kammakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Formal Acts)
1. The Act of Rebuke.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
At one time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, being themselves makers of strife, quarrels, disputes, and contention,

and instigators of legal issues in the Saṅgha, approached other monks who were likewise makers of strife, quarrels, disputes, and contention, and instigators of legal issues in the Saṅgha, and spoke to them thus:
“Venerable friends, do not let him defeat you.
Deliberate upon who is stronger and who is weaker.
You are more wise, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he.”
"Do not be afraid.
We too shall become your allies.
Because of this, quarrels that have not yet arisen come into being, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
Those bhikkhus who were few in desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can the bhikkhus Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka themselves be makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention,
and creators of legal issues in the Saṅgha, as well as other bhikkhus who are makers of strife and makers of quarrels?”
Those who cause disputes, those who engage in frivolous talk, and those who create legal issues within the Saṅgha will approach them and say:
“Venerable sirs, do not let this person defeat you.
Debate with him by weighing the strength and weakness of your arguments.”
"You are more wise, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he.
Do not be afraid of him;
we too shall become your allies."
“Because of that, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of bhikkhus assembled and questioned the bhikkhus:
“Is it true, monks, that the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, being themselves makers of strife,
makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha,
approached other monks who were also makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha, and spoke to them thus?”
“Venerable sirs, do not let him defeat you.
Weigh strength against strength.
You are wiser, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he.”
"Do not be afraid.
We too shall become your allies.
Because of this, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion. Is it not so?
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“Bhikkhus, it is unbecoming for those foolish men, it is unsuitable, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.”
"How indeed, monks, can those foolish men, being themselves quarrelsome... [and so on]...
creators of legal disputes in the Saṅgha, approach other monks who are also quarrelsome...
[and so on]... creators of legal disputes in the Saṅgha, and speak to them thus:"
“Venerable friends, do not let him defeat you.
Weigh strength against strength.
You are wiser, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he.”
"Do not be afraid.
We too shall become your allies.
It is by this that quarrels which have not yet arisen come into being, and quarrels which have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence, nor to the increase of confidence in those who already have it.
On the contrary, monks, this leads to the lack of confidence in those without confidence, and to the alienation of some among those who have confidence.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked those monks in many ways for their difficulty in being supported and their difficulty in being nourished...
Having spoken in many ways on the dispraise of great desire, discontent, socializing, and laziness, and having spoken in many ways on the praise of being easy to support,
easy to satisfy, of fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, the ascetic qualities, serenity,
reduction of worldly concerns, and the arousal of energy, he [taught] the monks what was suitable and appropriate for that.
Having given a talk on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, let the Saṅgha carry out a censure transaction against the bhikkhus Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
And this, bhikkhus, is how it should be done.”

First, the Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka bhikkhus should be charged; having been charged, they should be reminded; having been reminded, the offense should be laid against them; and having the offense laid against them, a competent and capable bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
These Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka bhikkhus are themselves makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, and makers of contention."
Those who create legal disputes in the Saṅgha, and whatever other bhikkhus there may be who are quarrelsome,
contentious, disputatious, and argumentative— those who create legal disputes in the Saṅgha— they approach them and speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, do not let this one defeat you.”
Deliberate upon what is strong and what is weak.
You are more wise, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he;
do not be afraid of him.
“We too shall become partisans of yours.
Because of this, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha carry out a censure transaction against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs.
These monks, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, are themselves quarrelsome... [and so forth].
Those who create legal disputes in the Saṅgha, as well as other monks who are quarrelsome... [and so on] ...those who create legal disputes in the Saṅgha, having approached them, speak thus:
"Venerable sirs, do not let this one defeat you."
Consult with one another regarding what is strong and what is weak.
You are more wise, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he;
do not be afraid of him.
“We too shall become partisans of yours.
Because of this, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
The Saṅgha then carries out a censure transaction against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
Whichever venerable one approves of the performance of the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
For a second time I speak this matter: [same as above].
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
These monks, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, are themselves makers of strife...
[and] makers of legal disputes in the Saṅgha."
And when other monks who were quarrelsome... [and] who created legal disputes in the Saṅgha approached them and spoke thus:
“Venerable sirs, do not let this one defeat you.
Debate him back, weighing strength against weakness.”
"You are more wise, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he.
Do not be afraid of him;
we too shall become your allies."
Because of this, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and expansion.
The Saṅgha is performing an act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the performance of the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, let him remain silent.
Whoever does not approve of this, let him speak.
For a third time I state this matter:
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, listen to me.
These monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, being themselves makers of strife...
[and] makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha, approached other monks who were also makers of strife... [and] makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha, and spoke to them thus:
“Venerable sirs, do not let him defeat you.
Deliberate upon what is strong and what is weak;
for you are wiser, more competent, more learned, and more capable than he.”
"Do not be afraid.
We too shall become your allies.
Because of this, quarrels that have not yet arisen arise, and quarrels that have already arisen lead to further increase and proliferation.
The Saṅgha is performing an act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of performing the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The Saṅgha has performed a censure transaction against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
1.1. The Group of Twelve on Transactions Contrary to the Dhamma.
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is carried out in the absence of the accused, it is carried out without having questioned him, and it is carried out without his admission.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.

It is carried out against one who has committed no offense; it is carried out against one who has committed an offense that does not require confession; it is carried out against one who has already confessed the offense.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is done without having charged [the person], it is done without having reminded [them of the offense], and it is done without having formally laid the charge of an offense.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is carried out in the absence of the accused, it is carried out contrary to the Dhamma, and it is carried out by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is done without having questioned [the accused], it is done illegitimately, and it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* possessing these three factors is an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is done without the consent [of the accused], it is done contrary to the Dhamma, and it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* possessing these three factors is an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is done in the absence of an offense, it is done illegitimately, and it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* possessing these three factors is an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is one performed for an offense that does not lead to confession; it is performed illegitimately; it is performed by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is performed for an offense that has been confessed; it is performed illegitimately; and it is performed by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses another three factors is also an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is carried out without having charged [the person], it is carried out illegitimately, and it is carried out by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) that possesses three other factors is also an illegal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is done without having brought [the accused] to account, it is done contrary to the Dhamma, and it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a *tajjanīya-kamma* possessing these three factors is an illegal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
“Monks, a procedure of censure that possesses three other factors is also an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
It is done without having charged an offense, it is done illegitimately, and it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a procedure of censure possessing these three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
The Group of Twelve on Invalid Legal Acts is finished.

1.2. The Group of Twelve on Valid Legal Acts “Monks, when a legal act of censure possesses three factors, it is a valid legal act, a legal act in accordance with the Vinaya, and one that is properly settled.
“It has been performed in the presence [of the accused], it has been performed with interrogation, and it has been performed with admission.
Monks, when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is properly settled.”
It is done regarding an offense; it is done regarding an offense that is subject to confession; it is done regarding an offense that has not been confessed.
Monks, when a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a *tajjanīya-kamma* possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled.
It is done after having charged [the monk]; it is done after having reminded [him]; it is done after having laid the offense [upon him].
Monks, when a censure transaction possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate transaction, a disciplinary transaction, and well-settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a censure transaction possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate transaction, a disciplinary transaction, and well-settled.
“It has been done in the presence [of the accused], it has been done according to the Dhamma, and it has been done by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is well-settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is well-settled.”
It is done after questioning; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a censure action possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate action, a disciplinary action, and one that is well-settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a censure action possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate action, a disciplinary action, and one that is well-settled.
It is done with the admission of the accused, it is done in accordance with the Dhamma, and it is done by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is properly settled.
“It has been done for an offense; it has been done in accordance with the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is well-settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is well-settled.”
When an offense is one that admits of confession, it is done in accordance with the Dhamma, and it is done by a unanimous assembly— monks,
when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is well-settled. Furthermore, monks,
when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is well-settled.
When an offense has been pointed out, it is done in accordance with the Dhamma, and it is done by a unanimous assembly— monks,
when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and one that is well-settled. Furthermore, monks,
when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and one that is well-settled.
When it has been done after summoning, it is done in accordance with the Dhamma, and it is done by a unanimous assembly— monks,
when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and well-settled. Furthermore, monks,
when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and well-settled.
"It has been carried out after having reminded [the accused]; it has been carried out in accordance with the Dhamma; it has been carried out by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a procedure of censure possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is well-settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a procedure of censure possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is well-settled."
It is done after having charged him with an offense; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a censure transaction possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate transaction, a disciplinary transaction, and well-settled.
The "Twelvefold Set on Legitimate Transactions" is finished.
1.3. The Sixfold Set on Wishing “Monks, when a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction against him:
he is a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a creator of legal issues in the Saṅgha.”
He is foolish, incompetent, full of offenses, and has not made amends for them;
he dwells in association with householders in inappropriate ways of associating with householders.
Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a censure transaction against a monk who possesses these three factors.
“Furthermore, monks, if a monk possesses three other qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction against him.
He has failed in higher virtue; he has failed in conduct regarding his behavior; he has failed in view regarding excessive views.
Monks, if a monk possesses these three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction against him.”
“Monks, when a monk possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction against him.
He speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction against him.”
“Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform a censure transaction against three kinds of monks:
one who is a creator of quarrels, a creator of strife, a creator of disputes, a creator of contention, and a creator of legal issues in the Saṅgha;
and one who is foolish, incompetent, full of offenses, and lacking in restoration.”
One who dwells in association with householders, engaging in improper forms of association with householders—
for these three kinds of monks, O bhikkhus, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction (tajjanīya-kamma).
Furthermore, O bhikkhus, for another three kinds of monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction.
One has failed in virtue regarding higher morality; one has failed in conduct regarding improper behavior; one has failed in view regarding excessive views.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction against these three monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a censure transaction against another three monks.
One speaks dispraise of the Buddha; one speaks dispraise of the Dhamma; one speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a censure transaction against these three monks.
The "Six on Desiring" is finished.
1.4. Eighteen Duties.
Monks, a monk against whom a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) has been carried out should conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
One should not grant full ordination,
one should not give formal support,
and one should not have a novice attend upon oneself.
The authorization to exhort bhikkhunīs must not be accepted,
nor should one who has been authorized exhort bhikkhunīs.
One must not commit the same offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out a censure transaction (tajjanīyakamma).
Whether it be another such as that,
or even more blameworthy than that,
one's action should not be censured.
The officiants are not to be censured.
The Uposatha should not be suspended for a regular monk,
nor should the Pavāraṇā be suspended.
One should not address him with words of censure,
nor should a formal accusation be raised against him,
nor should he be made to grant an opportunity for a legal procedure.
"He is not to be exhorted,
not to be reminded,
and not to be associated with by the monks."
The eighteen points of conduct regarding the act of censure are concluded.
1.5. The Group of Eighteen on What Should Not Be Stilled.
Then the Saṅgha performed an act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
Those who had been subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of censure behaved properly, lowered their hair (in humility), and conducted themselves toward deliverance. They approached the monks and said:
“Friends, we have been subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of censure; we behave properly, lower our hair, and conduct ourselves toward deliverance. How, then, should we proceed?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. …
“… Therefore, monks, let the Saṅgha rescind the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka. Monks,
the act of censure against a monk who possesses five qualities should not be rescinded.”
He ordains others; he gives formal support (nissaya); he has a novice attend upon him; he accepts appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he instructs the bhikkhunīs.
Monks, a censure transaction (tajjanīya-kamma) against a monk endowed with these five factors should not be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, a censure transaction against a monk endowed with another five factors should not be lifted.
If a monk commits the same offense for which the Saṅgha carried out the act of censure against him, or another similar offense, or one more serious than that;
if he criticizes the legal procedure and criticizes those who performed it—
monks, when a monk possesses these five factors, the act of censure against him must not be lifted.
“Monks, the act of censure against a monk who possesses eight factors should not be lifted.
He cancels the Uposatha of a regular monk; he cancels the Pavāraṇā; he makes himself subject to being spoken to; he initiates a formal accusation; he demands an opportunity [to speak];
he reproaches; he reminds; he associates with other monks. Monks, the act of censure against a monk who possesses these eight factors should not be lifted.”
The Section of Eighteens on What Should Not Be Revoked is finished.
1.6. The Section of Eighteens on What Should Be Revoked:
"Monks, the act of censure against a monk endowed with five factors should be revoked."
He does not grant full ordination; he does not give formal support; he does not have a novice attend him; he does not accept appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs;
and even when appointed, he does not instruct the bhikkhunīs—monks, a monk endowed with these five factors should have the act of censure suspended against him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with another five factors should have the act of censure suspended against him.
If a monk does not commit that offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out a procedure of censure, nor another similar one, nor one more serious than that;
and if he does not criticize the legal act,
nor criticize those who performed it— monks, the procedure of censure against a monk endowed with these five factors should be lifted.
“Monks, the act of censure against a monk endowed with eight factors should be lifted.

He does not cancel the Uposatha of a regular monk; he does not cancel the invitation ceremony; he does not issue commands; he does not initiate a formal charge; he does not demand an opportunity for an interview; he does not accuse; he does not remind;
he does not associate with other monks—it is when a monk is endowed with these eight factors, monks, that the act of censure should be lifted.”
The Section on the Eighteen Points for Settling is finished.
And furthermore, monks, it should be settled in this way:
Those monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, having approached the Saṅgha, should arrange their upper robes over one shoulder...
Having paid homage at the feet of the senior bhikkhus, sat down on his heels, and raised his joined palms, he should speak thus:

"Venerable sirs, we who have been subjected to a procedure of censure by the Saṅgha are conducting ourselves properly, acting in accordance with the requirements, and behaving so as to deserve release; we ask for the lifting of the procedure of censure.
He should ask a second time as well.
A third time she should be asked.
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.”

These monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, having been subjected by the Saṅgha to an act of censure, are conducting themselves properly; they are acting in accordance with the requirements, they are behaving so as to deserve release, and they request the lifting of the act of censure.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha lift the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.

These monks, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, who were subjected to a censure transaction by the Sangha, are now conducting themselves properly, lowering their hair, and behaving in a manner that leads to their rehabilitation; they request the lifting of the censure transaction.
The Sangha lifts the censure transaction against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka."
Whichever venerable one approves of the lifting of the procedure of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
For the second time, I speak this matter.
"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.

These monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, having been subjected to a censure transaction by the Sangha, are conducting themselves properly, they are lowering their hair [in humility], they are conducting themselves so as to deserve release, and they ask for the lifting of the censure transaction.
The Sangha lifts the censure transaction against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka."
Whichever venerable one approves of the revocation of the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
For the third time I state this matter:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.

These monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, having been subjected to a censure transaction by the Saṅgha, are conducting themselves properly, they are lowering their hair [in submission], they are conducting themselves so as to deserve release, and they ask for the lifting of the censure transaction.
The Saṅgha lifts the censure transaction against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka."
Whichever venerable one approves of the lifting of the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Sangha has lifted the act of censure against the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
"It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
The first section on the act of censure is concluded.
2. The Act of Subordination (Niyassakamma).
Now at that time, the Venerable Seyyasaka was foolish, incompetent, prone to offenses, and lacking in rehabilitation;
he lived in association with householders through improper associations with householders.
Furthermore, the monks were busy granting probation, sending back to the beginning, granting the *mānatta* penance, and rehabilitating him.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the venerable Seyyasaka be so foolish, incompetent, full of offenses, and lacking in restraint;
how can he dwell in association with householders through improper associations with householders?”
“Moreover, monks, there were monks who, while granting probation, sending back to the beginning, granting the trial period (mānatta), or rehabilitating [an offender], acted improperly.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that the monk Seyyasaka is foolish, incompetent, prone to offenses, and lacking in restraint;
that he lives in association with householders through improper forms of association with householders;
and that even when other monks are formally processing him—granting probation, sending back to the beginning, granting the trial period, or rehabilitating him?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“Monks, it is unbecoming, unsuitable, unworthy, improper, unseemly, and not to be done by that foolish man.”
"How indeed, monks, can that foolish, incompetent man be so full of offenses and unrestrained;
how can he dwell in association with householders through improper associations with householders;
and how can he even cause the monks who have been formally dealt with to undergo probation, to be sent back to the beginning, to undergo the trial period, or to be rehabilitated?"
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:”
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha carry out a formal act of subordination against the monk Seyyasaka, [pronouncing]:
‘You must live in dependence.
And this, monks, is how it should be done.

First, the monk Seyyasaka should be reproved; having been reproved, he should be reminded; having been reminded, he should be charged with an offense; having been charged with an offense, the Saṅgha should be informed by a competent and capable monk:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
This monk Seyyasaka is foolish, incompetent, full of offenses, and lacking in restraint."
He lives in association with householders through improper associations with householders;

moreover, he causes even those monks who have been properly dealt with to be sent back to the beginning when granting probation, sending back to the beginning when granting a trial period, or granting rehabilitation.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha carry out an act of demotion against the monk Seyyasaka.
"You must dwell depending on them.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs.
This bhikkhu Seyyasaka is foolish, incompetent, prone to offenses, and lacking in restoration;
he lives in association with householders through improper associations with householders;
and even while the bhikkhus are acting rightly—granting him probation, sending him back to the beginning, granting him the *mānatta* penance, or rehabilitating him—he persists in this behavior.
The Saṅgha is performing an act of subordination against the bhikkhu Seyyasaka:
"You must live in dependence.
To whichever venerable one the performance of this act of subordination against the bhikkhu Seyyasaka is agreeable—
"You should dwell depending on them. He who approves of this should remain silent;
he who does not approve should speak.
For a second time, I speak this matter... [as before]...
For a third time I speak on this matter:
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
This monk Seyyasaka is foolish, incompetent, full of offenses, and unrestrained.
He lived in association with householders in unbecoming ways.
Furthermore, while the monks were granting probation, sending back to the beginning, granting the trial period (mānatta), and rehabilitating others, they did the same for the monk Seyyasaka.
The Saṅgha performed an act of demotion against the monk Seyyasaka.
"You must live in dependence upon them.
Whichever venerable one approves of performing the act of demotion against the monk Seyyasaka—
[with the motion] "You must live in dependence upon them"— let him be silent.
Whoever does not agree with this may speak.
The Sangha has performed the act of demotion against the monk Seyyasaka:

“It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this. 2.1.

“It is done in the absence of the person concerned; it is done without having questioned [the accused]; it is done without the admission [of the accused].

Furthermore, monks, a *niyassa-kamma* endowed with another three factors is an illegal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.”
It is done for one who has committed no offense; it is done for one who has committed an offense that does not require confession; it is done for one who has already confessed the offense.

Furthermore, monks, a *niyassa* legal act endowed with another three factors is an illegitimate legal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.

2.2. The Group of Twelve on Legitimate Legal Acts “Monks, a legal act of demotion that possesses three factors is a legitimate legal act, a legal act in accordance with the Vinaya, and one that is well-settled.
It is done in the presence [of the accused], it is done after interrogation, and it is done with the admission [of the accused].”
“Monks, when it possesses these three factors, a *niyassa* (rehabilitation) legal procedure is a legitimate legal procedure, a disciplinary legal procedure, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when it possesses another three factors, a *niyassa* legal procedure is a legitimate legal procedure, a disciplinary legal procedure, and is properly settled:
it is carried out for an offense; it is carried out for an offense that is subject to confession; it is carried out for an offense that has not been confessed.”
“Monks, when it possesses these three factors, a *niyassa* (rehabilitation) legal act is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when it possesses another three factors, a *niyassa* legal act is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled:
it is done after having charged [the offender], it is done after having reminded [him of his offense], and it is done after having formally charged him with the offense.”
“Monks, when a formal act of demotion possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled. Furthermore, monks,
[it is also] one that has been carried out in the presence [of the accused], carried out according to the Dhamma, and carried out by a unanimous assembly.”

2.3. The ‘Set of Six on Those Who Wish’”
“Monks, when a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of demotion against him:
he is a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a maker of legal issues in the Saṅgha;
he is foolish, incompetent, full of offenses, and lacking in restoration.”
He dwells in association with householders through improper forms of association with householders.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of demotion against him.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of demotion against him.
He is failed in virtue regarding higher virtue, he is failed in conduct regarding proper conduct, and he is failed in view regarding extreme views—
it is when a bhikkhu possesses these three factors, monks, that the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of demotion against him. Furthermore, monks,
when a bhikkhu possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of demotion against him.
"He speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha—
it is when a bhikkhu is possessed of these three factors, monks, that the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of demotion against him.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of demotion against three kinds of bhikkhus."
One is a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a creator of legal issues in the Saṅgha;
one is foolish, incompetent, prone to offenses, and lacking in restoration;
one dwells in association with householders through improper forms of association with householders.
"Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform a formal act of demotion against these three kinds of monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform a formal act of demotion against another three kinds of monks:
one who has failed in virtue regarding higher morality, one who has failed in conduct regarding his behavior, and one who has failed in view regarding his perspective."
“Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of demotion against these three kinds of monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of demotion against another three kinds of monks:
one who speaks dispraise of the Buddha, one who speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and one who speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.”
“Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of demotion against these three monks.
The ‘Six on Desire’ is finished.

The Group of Eighteen on What Should Not Be Rescinded”
“Monks, the act of censure (niyassakamma) against a monk endowed with five factors should not be lifted.

He ordains others; he gives formal support (nissaya); he has a novice attend upon him; he consents to being appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he instructs the bhikkhunīs.
Monks, the act of censure against a monk endowed with these five factors should not be lifted.”
“Monks, the act of demotion (niyassakamma) against a monk who possesses five other qualities should not be lifted. These are:
he commits the same offense for which the Sangha performed the act of demotion, or another offense similar to it, or one more serious than it;
he criticizes the legal procedure, and he criticizes those who carried out the procedure.”
Monks, the act of demotion (niyassakamma) for a monk endowed with these five factors should not be lifted.
Monks, the act of demotion for a monk endowed with eight factors should not be lifted:

he cancels the Uposatha of a regular monk; he cancels the Pavāraṇā; he makes himself subject to being spoken to; he initiates a formal accusation; he demands an opportunity [to speak]; he reproaches; he reminds; he involves himself in disputes with other monks.
Monks, the formal act of censure (niyassakamma) against a monk who possesses these eight factors is not to be lifted.

he does not criticize the legal procedure, nor does he criticize those who performed it.”
Monks, the act of demotion (*niyassakamma*) should be lifted for a monk who possesses these five factors.

3. The Act of Banishment.
Now at that time, there were certain monks named Assaji and Punabbasuka who resided at Kīṭāgiri; they were shameless and evil monks.
They practiced such improper conduct as this:
They plant jasmine vines themselves or have them planted; they water them themselves or have them watered; they pluck them themselves or have them plucked;
they string them themselves or have them strung; they make single-stalk garlands themselves or have them made; they make double-stalk garlands themselves or have them made;
they make cluster-garlands themselves or have them made; they make hanging-garlands themselves or have them made.
They themselves make ear-ornaments and have them made; they themselves make garlands for the head and have them made; they themselves make breast-plates and have them made.

They themselves carry single-stalked garlands and have them carried [for] women of good family, daughters of good family, young girls of good family, daughters-in-law of good family, and female slaves of good family;
they themselves carry double-stalked garlands and have them carried; they themselves carry flower-clusters... and have them carried.
They take away [ornaments], they take away the *vidhūtika* themselves or have it taken away; they take away the *vaṭaṃsaka* themselves or have it taken away;
they take away the *āveḷa* themselves or have it taken away; they take away the breast-cloth (*uracchada*) themselves or have it taken away.
They [dine] even from the same vessel together with women of good family, daughters of good family, young maidens of good family, daughters-in-law of good family, and female slaves of good family.

They eat together, they drink from the same bowl, they sit on the same seat, they lie down on the same couch, they lie down on the same bedspread, they lie down under the same cloak, they lie down on the same bedspread and cloak;
they eat at improper times, they drink intoxicants, they wear garlands, scents, and ointments; they dance and they sing.
They play instruments for her, they dance for her;
when she dances, they dance; when she dances, they sing; when she dances, they play instruments; when she dances, they dance.
When she sings, they dance; when she sings, they sing; when she sings, they play instruments; when she sings, they dance.

While one plays an instrument, another dances; while one plays an instrument, another sings; while one plays an instrument, another plays an instrument; while one plays an instrument, another performs a dance.
While one performs a dance, another dances; while one performs a dance, another sings; while one performs a dance, another plays an instrument; while one performs a dance, another performs a dance.
They play at eight-row checkers, they play at ten-row checkers, they play in the air, and they play on a narrow path.
They play with sandcastles, they play with pebbles, they play with clay pots, they play with counting-slips held in the hand,
they play with dice, they play with rag-puppets, they play with crooked sticks, they play with top-spinners,
they play with whirlwinds, they play with leaf-bowls, they play with toy chariots, and they play with toy bows.
They play with alphabet games, they play with mental exercises, and they play with mimicry;
they train in elephant-riding, they train in horsemanship, they train in charioteering, they train in archery, and they train in swordsmanship;
they run in front of elephants, they run in front of horses, and they even run alongside and charge along with chariots.
They shout, they clap their hands, they wrestle, and they fight with their fists;
even in the middle of a stage, having spread out their outer robes, they say to a dancer, "Dance here, sister!"
They even give forehead marks;
they practice various kinds of improper conduct.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu who had completed the rains retreat among the Kāsīs was traveling toward Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One and arrived at Kīṭāgiri.
Then, in the morning, that bhikkhu dressed and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kīṭāgiri for alms.
He was pleasing in his advance and retreat, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching;
with downcast eyes, he was perfected in his deportment.
When people saw that bhikkhu, they said:
"Where has this man come from, looking so weak and feeble, so dull and sluggish, with such a frowning face?
Who will give even a morsel of almsfood to one who has approached us like this?"
"But our masters Assaji and Punabbasu are gentle, courteous, pleasant to speak with, preceded by smiles, speakers of welcome, free from frowns, open-faced, and the first to speak.
Alms should indeed be given to them.
Then a certain lay follower saw that monk wandering for alms at Kīṭāgiri.
Having seen him, he approached that bhikkhu; having approached and paid homage to that bhikkhu, he said this:
"Venerable sir, has alms been obtained?
"Indeed, friend, no alms have been obtained."
“Come, venerable sir, let us go to my home.
Then that lay follower, having led the bhikkhu to his home and fed him, said this:
“Where will the noble one go, venerable sir?”
“I am going to Sāvatthī, friend, to see the Blessed One.
“In that case, venerable sir, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Blessed One in my name, and say this:
‘Venerable sir, the dwelling place at Kīṭāgiri is corrupt.’”
The monks known as Assaji and Punabbasuka were shameless, evil bhikkhus who resided at Kīṭāgiri.
They engaged in such improper conduct as this:
they planted flowering shrubs themselves or had them planted; they watered them themselves or had them watered; they gathered flowers themselves or had them gathered.
They themselves tie them together and have others tie them together; they themselves make garlands with a single stalk and have others make them;

they themselves make garlands with stalks on both sides and have others make them; they themselves make cluster-garlands and have others make them; they themselves make hanging-garlands and have others make them;
they themselves make ear-ornaments and have others make them; they themselves make head-crests and have others make them; they themselves make breast-chains and have others make them.
They themselves carry, or cause others to carry, single-stalked garlands for noble women, daughters of noble families, noble maidens, noble daughters-in-law, and noble female slaves;
they themselves carry, or cause others to carry, double-stalked garlands; they themselves carry, or cause others to carry, flower-clusters;
they themselves carry, or cause others to carry, loose flowers; they themselves carry, or cause others to carry, ear-ornaments.
They take away hair ornaments, or have them taken away; they take away breast-cloths, or have them taken away.
They eat from the same vessel as women of good family, daughters of good family, young girls of good family, daughters-in-law of good family, and female slaves of good family;
they drink from the same water-pot; they sit on the same seat; they lie down on the same couch; they share the same blanket.
They lie down together; they lie down with only a single upper garment; they lie down with a single bed-covering and upper garment;
they eat at improper times; they drink intoxicants; they wear garlands, scents, and ointments;
they dance, sing, play instruments, and perform on stage.
While she was dancing, they danced; while she was dancing, they sang; while she was dancing, they played instruments; while she was dancing, they performed a dance… (the wheel should be constructed).

While she was performing a dance, they danced; while she was performing a dance, they sang; while she was performing a dance, they played instruments; while she was performing a dance, they performed a dance.
They played at eight-row chess, they played at ten-row chess, they played in the air, they played on the path of circumambulation,

even in the middle of the arena, having spread out their outer robes, they say this to a dancer:
“Come here, sister, and dance,” they say;
they even give her a wager,

"Those people, venerable sir, who formerly had faith and confidence have now become faithless and lacking in confidence.
Those gifts that were formerly bestowed upon the Saṅgha have now been cut off.
Virtuous bhikkhus are being neglected, while wicked bhikkhus dwell there."
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would send monks to Kīṭāgiri, so that this monastery at Kīṭāgiri may become firmly established.
“Very well, friend,” that monk replied to the lay follower, rose from his seat, and set out for Sāvatthī.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Sāvatthī, at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, where he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting monks.
Then the Blessed One said this to that monk:
"I hope, monk, that you are bearing up; I hope you are getting along."
“I hope you have come along this road without fatigue;
from where, monk, do you come?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is livable, Blessed One.”
"And I have come along this road, venerable sir, without fatigue.
Here, venerable sir, having spent the rains retreat among the Kāsīs, I was coming to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One when I stayed at Kīṭāgiri.
Then, venerable sir, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Kīṭāgiri for alms."
“Venerable sir, a certain lay follower saw me while I was walking for alms at Kīṭāgiri;
having seen me, he approached me, paid homage to me, and said this:
‘Venerable sir, has any alms been obtained?’”
“Friend, no alms-food was obtained.
“Come, venerable sir, let us go to the house.
Then, venerable sir, that lay follower led me to his house, fed me, and said this:
“Where, venerable sir, will the master go?
“I shall go to Sāvatthī, friend, to see the Blessed One.
“In that case, venerable sir, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Blessed One in my name, and say this:”
“Venerable sir, the monastery at Kīṭāgiri is corrupt.

They plant flowering trees themselves, or have them planted...

“Those former sources of offerings for the Saṅgha have now been cut off.

It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would send bhikkhus to Kīṭāgiri, so that this residence at Kīṭāgiri may be stabilized.”
“From there, Blessed One, I am coming.
Then, on this occasion and for this reason, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that those known as Assaji and Punabbasu, who are residents at Kīṭāgiri, are shameless and evil monks?”
Do they practice such improper conduct as planting flowering shrubs...
[and so on] ...practicing various kinds of improper conduct?
“Are those people who were formerly faithful and confident now faithless and lacking confidence?
Are those former paths of giving to the Saṅgha now cut off?
Do virtuous bhikkhus neglect it, while wicked bhikkhus dwell there?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unbecoming... [as before]...”
"How indeed, monks, can those foolish men practice such improper conduct as this—they will plant flower seedlings or have them planted;
they will water them or have them watered; they will pluck them or have them plucked;
they will string them or have them strung; they will make garlands with single stalks."
They will also have [garlands] made; they will make double-stalked garlands and have them made;
they will make cluster-garlands and have them made; they will make hanging-garlands and have them made;
they will make ear-ornaments and have them made; they will make head-bands and have them made; they will make breast-covers and have them made.
He will carry, or cause to be carried, single-stalked garlands for noble women, daughters of noble families, noble maidens, noble daughters-in-law, and noble female slaves;
he will carry, or cause to be carried, double-stalked garlands; he will carry, or cause to be carried, cluster-garlands;
he will carry, or cause to be carried, loose-flowers; he will carry, or cause to be carried, hair-ornaments.
They will take away garlands themselves, or have them taken away; they will take away breast-cloths themselves, or have them taken away.
They will eat from the same vessel as noble women, noble daughters, noble maidens, noble daughters-in-law, and noble slave-girls;
they will drink from the same water-jar; they will sit on the same seat; and they will lie down on the same couch.
They will lie down on a single spread, they will lie down under a single coverlet, they will lie down with a single spread and coverlet;
they will eat at improper times, they will drink intoxicants, they will wear garlands, scents, and unguents;
they will dance, they will sing, they will play music, and they will cause others to dance.
While she is dancing, they will dance; while she is dancing, they will sing; while she is dancing, they will play instruments; while she is dancing, they will cause her to laugh.
While she is singing, they will dance; while she is singing, they will sing; while she is singing, they will play instruments; while she is singing, they will cause her to laugh.

While she is playing instruments, they will dance; while she is playing instruments, they will sing; while she is playing instruments, they will play instruments; while she is playing instruments, they will cause her to laugh.
They will dance with lāsentiya, they will sing with lāsentiya, they will play music with lāsentiya,
and they will cause others to sport with lāsentiya; they will play at eight-row chess, they will play at ten-row chess, they will play in the air,
they will play on the path of circumambulation, they will play at santikā, they will play at khalikā, and they will play at ghaṭikā.
They will play with sticks in their hands; they will play with dice; they will play with cloth strips; they will play with crooked sticks; they will play with top-spinners;
they will play with whirling disks; they will play with leaf-cups; they will play with toy chariots; they will play with toy bows;
they will play with letter-games; they will play with guessing-thoughts.
They will play, and they will play even with vulgar games;
they will train in elephant-riding, they will train in horsemanship, they will train in charioteering, they will train in archery, and they will train in swordsmanship;
they will run ahead of elephants, they will run ahead of horses, and they will both run alongside and charge ahead of chariots.
They will shout out, they will clap their hands, they will wrestle, and they will fight with their fists;
even on the stage, having spread out their outer robes, they will say to a dancer, “Dance here, sister!”
They will even wear forehead marks;
they will practice various kinds of improper conduct.
(…) This, monks, does not lead to the inspiration of those without faith, nor to the increase of those with faith... [and so on].
Having rebuked them … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna:
“Go, Sāriputtas, go to Kīṭāgiri and carry out an act of banishment against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka from Kīṭāgiri; these were your co-residents.”
“Venerable sir, how should we carry out the act of banishment against the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka from Kīṭāgiri? Those bhikkhus are fierce and harsh.
“In that case, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, you should go together with many bhikkhus.
“Very well, venerable sir,” Sāriputta and Moggallāna replied to the Blessed One.
“And furthermore, monks, it should be done as follows:

first, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are to be accused; having been accused, they are to be reminded; having been reminded, the offense is to be charged; having the offense charged, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. [...]*’” (*The rest of the formal motion follows).
These monks, Assaji and Punabbasuka, are corrupters of families and of evil conduct.
Their evil conduct is both seen and heard of;
and families corrupted by them are both seen and heard of.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha carry out an act of banishment against the monks Assaji and Punabbasu from Kīṭāgiri,
so that the monks Assaji and Punabbasu shall not dwell at Kīṭāgiri.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
These monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are corrupters of families and of evil conduct.
Their evil conduct is both seen and heard."
And families corrupted by these [monks] are both seen and heard of.
The Sangha is performing an act of banishment against the monks Assaji and Punabbasu from Kīṭāgiri, [deciding]:
"The monks Assaji and Punabbasu must not dwell at Kīṭāgiri."

Venerable sirs, whichever venerable one approves of the performance of the act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka—so that the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka shall not dwell at Kīṭāgiri—let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak on this matter... [as before]...
For a third time I speak this matter:
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
These monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are corrupters of families and of evil conduct.
The evil conduct of these men is both seen and heard;
families corrupted by them are also both seen and heard.
The Saṅgha is performing an act of banishment against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka from Kīṭāgiri.
"The monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are not to dwell at Kīṭāgiri.

Whichever venerable one approves of performing the act of banishment against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka from Kīṭāgiri—so that the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka shall not dwell at Kīṭāgiri—let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The Saṅgha has performed an act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka—[the decree] that the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka must not dwell at Kīṭāgiri.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.”

3.1. The Group of Twelve on Invalid Legal Acts “Monks, a legal act of banishment that possesses three factors is an invalid legal act, a non-disciplinary legal act, and one that is not properly settled.
It is performed in the absence of the accused, it is performed without interrogation, and it is performed without the consent of the accused.”
“Monks, a formal act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*) that possesses these three factors is an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
Furthermore, monks, a formal act of banishment that possesses another three factors is an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled:

it is performed for one who has committed no offense; it is performed for one who has committed an offense that does not require confession; it is performed for one who has already confessed the offense. … [as above] …

It is done without having charged [the person]; it is done without having reminded [them]; it is done without having formally brought up the offense …pe… it is done in their absence; it is done contrary to the Dhamma;
it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done without interrogation; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…

It is done without the admission [of the offense]; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that is not an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma;
it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that does not require confession; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…
When an offense has been confessed, it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… when it is done without having charged [the offender],

it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… when it is done without having reminded [the offender], it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…
It is done without having charged him with an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, when a formal act of banishment possesses these three factors, it is an illegitimate legal act, it is contrary to the discipline, and it is not properly settled.
The Section of Twelve on Illegitimate Legal Acts is finished.

3.2. The Group of Twelve on Legal Acts Concerning Dhamma “Monks, when an act of banishment possesses three factors, it is a legal act according to the Dhamma, a legal act according to the Vinaya, and is properly settled:
it is done in the presence [of the accused], it is done after interrogation, and it is done with the admission [of the accused].”
“Monks, when a formal act of banishment possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when a formal act of banishment possesses another three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled:
it is done for an offense; it is done for an offense that is subject to confession; it is done for an offense that has not been confessed … [and so on].”
It has been done after having charged [the person]; it has been done after having reminded [them]; it has been done after having laid the offense [upon them] ...
[as above] ... it has been done in their presence; it has been done according to the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly ...
[as above] ... it has been done by way of questioning; it has been done according to the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly ... [as above].
It is done with the admission [of the offense]; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done for an offense; it is done according to the Dhamma;
it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that requires confession; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe…
It is done regarding an offense that has not been confessed; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma;
it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done after having charged [the person]; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma;
it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done after having reminded [the person]; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe…
It has been carried out after charging him with an offense; it has been carried out in accordance with the Dhamma; it has been carried out by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a formal act of banishment possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled.
The "Twelve on Legitimate Acts" is finished.
3.3. The Set of Fourteen on One Who Desires [to Be Sent Away] “Monks, when a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him:
he is a maker of strife, a maker of quarrels, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a maker of legal issues in the Saṅgha.”
He is foolish and incompetent, full of offenses and unwilling to make amends;
he dwells in association with householders through improper forms of association with householders.
Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may perform an act of banishment against a monk who possesses these three factors.
“Monks, when a monk possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.
He has failed in higher virtue; he has failed in conduct regarding his behavior; he has failed in view regarding extreme views.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.”
“Furthermore, monks, if a monk possesses three other qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of banishment against him.
He speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
Monks, if a monk possesses these three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of banishment against him.”
“Monks, when a monk possesses three other qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.
He is possessed of bodily frivolity, he is possessed of verbal frivolity, and he is possessed of both bodily and verbal frivolity.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.”
“Monks, when a monk possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.
He is possessed of bodily misconduct, he is possessed of verbal misconduct, and he is possessed of both bodily and verbal misconduct.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.”
“Furthermore, monks, if a monk possesses three other qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.
He is possessed of bodily harmfulness; he is possessed of verbal harmfulness; he is possessed of both bodily and verbal harmfulness.
Monks, if a monk possesses these three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.”
“Furthermore, monks, when a monk possesses three other qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.
He is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of body, he is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of speech, and he is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of both body and speech.
When a monk possesses these three qualities, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against him.”
“Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of banishment against three kinds of monks:
one who is quarrelsome, contentious, argumentative, disputatious, and a creator of legal issues in the Saṅgha;
and one who is ignorant, incompetent, prone to offenses, and lacking in restraint.”
One who dwells in association with householders, engaging in improper forms of association with householders—
of these three kinds of monks, O bhikkhus, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment.
Furthermore, O bhikkhus, of another three kinds of monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment.
One has failed in virtue regarding higher morality; one has failed in conduct regarding improper behavior; one has failed in view regarding extreme views.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a procedure of banishment against these three kinds of monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a procedure of banishment against another three kinds of monks.
One speaks dispraise of the Buddha, one speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and one speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha— of these three monks,
O bhikkhus, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment. Furthermore, O bhikkhus, of another three monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment.
One is possessed of bodily frivolity; one is possessed of verbal frivolity; one is possessed of both bodily and verbal frivolity.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against these three kinds of monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against another three kinds of monks.
One is possessed of misconduct by way of body; one is possessed of misconduct by way of speech; one is possessed of misconduct by way of both body and speech.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of banishment against these three kinds of monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of banishment against another three kinds of monks.
One is possessed of bodily harmfulness; one is possessed of verbal harmfulness; one is possessed of both bodily and verbal harmfulness.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against these three monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of banishment against another three monks.
One is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of body; one is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of speech; one is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of both body and speech.
Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a formal act of banishment against these three monks.
The "Set of Fourteen on Desire" is finished.
3.4. The Eighteen Kinds of Conduct.
Monks, a monk against whom a formal act of banishment has been carried out should conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
One should not grant full ordination,
one should not give formal support,
and one should not have a novice attend upon oneself.
The appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs must not be accepted;
even one who has been appointed must not instruct the bhikkhunīs.
One must not commit the same offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out an act of banishment against oneself.
Whether it be another such person or one even more wicked than that,
their action is not to be censured.
The officiants are not to be censured.
The Uposatha should not be suspended for a regular monk,
nor should the Pavāraṇā be suspended.
One should not address them with a formal admonition,
nor initiate a censure against them,
nor demand an opportunity for their defense.
"He is not to be exhorted,
not to be reminded,
and not to be associated with by the bhikkhus."
The eighteen duties regarding the formal act of banishment are concluded.
Then the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, went to Kīṭāgiri and performed the formal act of banishment against the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu:
"The bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu must not dwell at Kīṭāgiri."
Having been subjected by the Saṅgha to the formal act of banishment, they do not conduct themselves properly, they do not behave with humility, and they do not act toward their rehabilitation;
they do not ask the bhikkhus for forgiveness, but instead revile and abuse them;
they act out of favoritism, ill will, delusion, and fear.
They departed, and some even left the order.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:

"How can the monks Assaji and Punabbasu, having had a formal act of banishment carried out against them by the Saṅgha, neither conduct themselves properly, nor show respect, nor act toward a resolution?"
“They will not ask the monks for forgiveness; they will revile them, they will abuse them;
they will bring about favoritism, ill-will, delusion, and fear;
they will even depart or disrobe.”
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of bhikkhus assembled and questioned the bhikkhus:

"Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka, having been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of banishment, do not conduct themselves properly, do not behave in accordance with the Saṅgha’s wishes, and do not seek reconciliation?"
"Do they not ask forgiveness from the monks, but instead revile and abuse them;
do they not act out of favoritism, ill will, delusion, or fear;
and do they not even depart or disrobe?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unbecoming... [as before]...”

How indeed, monks, can those foolish men, having had a formal act of banishment carried out against them by the Saṅgha, not conduct themselves properly, not behave with humility, and not strive for their rehabilitation;
how can they fail to ask forgiveness from the monks, but instead revile and abuse them;
and how can they fall into being swayed by favoritism, ill-will, delusion, or fear?
They will depart, they will disrobe.
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him... [and so on].
Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
"In that case, bhikkhus, let the Saṅgha rescind the act of banishment. 3.5.
The Group of Eighteen on What Should Not Be Rescinded"
“Monks, the act of banishment against a monk endowed with five factors should not be lifted.
He ordains [others], he gives formal dependence, he has a novice attend to him, he consents to being appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs, and even when appointed, he instructs the bhikkhunīs.
Monks, the act of banishment against a monk endowed with these five factors should not be lifted.”
“Monks, a procedure of banishment against a monk who possesses five other qualities should not be lifted:
he commits the same offense for which the Sangha carried out the procedure of banishment, or another offense of a similar nature, or one more serious than that;
he criticizes the legal act, and he criticizes those who performed the legal act.”
Monks, the procedure of banishment against a monk endowed with these five factors should not be lifted.
Monks, the procedure of banishment against a monk endowed with eight factors should not be lifted:

he cancels the Uposatha of a regular monk; he cancels the Pavāraṇā; he makes himself subject to being spoken to; he initiates a formal accusation; he demands an opportunity [to speak]; he accuses; he reminds; he involves himself in disputes with other monks.
Monks, the procedure of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*) for a monk endowed with these eight factors is not to be suspended.
The section of eighteen points on when the procedure of banishment is not to be suspended is finished. 3.6.
The Section of Eighteen Points on When It Is to Be Suspended.
“Monks, the *pabbājanīya-kamma* (act of banishment) against a monk endowed with five factors should be lifted.

He does not ordain; he does not give formal support (*nissaya*); he does not have a novice attend upon him; he does not accept the appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he does not instruct the bhikkhunīs.
Monks, the *pabbājanīya-kamma* against a monk endowed with these five factors should be lifted.”
“Monks, a procedure of banishment against a monk who possesses five other qualities should be lifted:
he does not commit the offense for which the Sangha carried out the procedure of banishment, nor another offense of a similar kind, nor one more serious than that;
he does not criticize the legal act, nor does he criticize those who performed it.”
Monks, the act of banishment against a monk endowed with these five factors should be suspended.
Monks, the act of banishment against a monk endowed with eight factors should be suspended:

he does not cancel the Uposatha of a regular monk; he does not cancel the Pavāraṇā; he does not issue a formal command; he does not initiate a legal accusation; he does not demand an opportunity for an interview; he does not accuse; he does not remind; he does not associate with other monks.
Monks, the legal procedure of banishment against a monk endowed with these eight factors should be lifted.
The section of eighteen items concerning the lifting of the legal procedure of banishment is finished.
And furthermore, monks, it should be lifted in this way.

“Monks, that monk against whom the act of banishment has been carried out should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior monks, sit down on his heels, raise his joined palms, and speak as follows:

‘Venerable sirs, I, who have been subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of banishment, am conducting myself properly, I am showing humility, I am conducting myself so as to deserve release; I ask for the lifting of the act of banishment.’”
A second time she should be asked;

the Venerable Mahākaccāna, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, the Venerable Mahākappina, and the Venerable Mahācunda.
The Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Upāli, the Venerable Ānanda, and the Venerable Rāhula,

The householder Citta heard that the elder bhikkhus had indeed arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa.
Then Citta the householder approached the elder bhikkhus; having approached, he paid homage to the elder bhikkhus and sat down to one side.
As Citta the householder was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Sāriputta’s discourse on the Dhamma, Citta the householder said this to the elder bhikkhus:
“Venerable sirs, may the elders accept from me tomorrow’s meal for guests.
The elder monks accepted by remaining silent.
Then Citta the householder, understanding the elders’ acceptance, rose from his seat and approached the elders.
Having paid homage to the bhikkhus and kept them on his right, he approached the Venerable Sudhamma;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Sudhamma and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Citta the householder said this to the Venerable Sudhamma:
“Venerable sir, may the noble Sudhamma, together with the elders, accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow.
Then the Venerable Sudhamma thought:
“Previously, whenever this householder Citta wished to invite the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, he would never do so without first consulting me.”
Then, without taking leave of me, he invited the elder bhikkhus.

"When one wishes to rain like a hen, it rains 'hen-hen.

"You are reviling me, householder! You are insulting me, householder!"
“This is your dwelling, householder; I shall depart.
“Venerable sir, I do not revile or abuse Master Sudhamma.
