"The rose-apple grove is delightful.
I shall make an effort for the noble Sudhamma regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
For a second time... [as before]...
For a third time, the Venerable Sudhamma said this to the householder Citta:
“You revile me, householder; you abuse me, householder.
This is your dwelling, householder; I shall depart.”
“Venerable sir, where will the master Sudhamma go?
“I am going to Sāvatthī, householder, to see the Blessed One.
“In that case, venerable sir, please report everything to the Blessed One—both what you have said yourself and what I have said.”
"But it is not surprising, venerable sir, that the Venerable Sudhamma should return once more to Macchikāsaṇḍa.
Then the Venerable Sudhamma, having tidied his lodging, took his bowl and robe, and set out for Sāvatthī.
Traveling by stages, he approached Sāvatthī, the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, and the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Sudhamma reported to the Blessed One everything that he himself had said and everything that the householder Citta had said.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
"It is unseemly, foolish man, it is unbecoming, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done."
"How indeed, foolish man, could you revile and insult with disparaging words Citta the householder—who is faithful, confident, a donor, a benefactor, and an attendant of the Saṅgha?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...

This bhikkhu Sudhamma reviles and insults the householder Citta—who is faithful, confident, a donor, a benefactor, and an attendant of the Saṅgha—with base things.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha carry out an act of reconciliation against the bhikkhu Sudhamma, [pronouncing]:
"The householder Citta must be asked for forgiveness by you."
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs:
this bhikkhu Sudhamma reviles and insults with disparagement the householder Citta, who is faithful, confident, a donor, a benefactor, and an attendant of the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha performs an act of reconciliation against the bhikkhu Sudhamma, [saying]:
"Householder Citta must be asked for forgiveness by you.
Whichever venerable one approves of performing this act of reconciliation against the bhikkhu Sudhamma—[saying] "Householder Citta must be asked for forgiveness by you"—let him be silent.

‘Householder Citta must be asked for forgiveness by you.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.”

4.1. The Group of Twelve on Invalid Legal Acts “Monks, when a legal act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*) possesses three factors, it is an invalid legal act, contrary to the discipline, and not properly settled.
It is performed in the absence of the accused; it is performed without having questioned [the accused]; it is performed without the consent [of the accused].”
“Monks, a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (act of reconciliation) endowed with these three factors is an illegal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.
Furthermore, monks, a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* endowed with another three factors is an illegal act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled:

it is performed against one who has committed no offense; it is performed against one who has committed an offense that does not require confession; it is performed against one who has already confessed the offense... [as above] ...”
It is done without having charged [the person]; it is done without having reminded [them]; it is done without having laid a formal charge for an offense ...
[etc. ... it is done not in their presence; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly ...
[etc. ... it is done without interrogation; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly ... [etc. ...

It is done without the admission [of the offense]; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that is not an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma;
it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that does not require confession; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…
When an offense has been confessed, it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done without having charged [the offender],

it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done without having reminded [the offender], it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…
It is done without having charged him with an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, when a procedure of reconciliation possesses these three factors, it is an illegitimate legal procedure, it is contrary to the discipline, and it is not properly settled.
The group of twelve on illegitimate legal procedures regarding the procedure of reconciliation is finished.

4.2. The Group of Twelve on Legal Acts Concerning the Dhamma “Monks, a legal act of reconciliation that possesses three factors is a legal act in accordance with the Dhamma, a legal act in accordance with the Vinaya, and one that is well-settled.
It is performed in the presence [of the accused], it is performed after interrogation, and it is performed with the admission [of the fault].”
“Monks, when it possesses these three factors, a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (act of reconciliation) is a legal act according to the Dhamma, a legal act according to the Vinaya, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when it possesses another three factors, a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* is a legal act according to the Dhamma, a legal act according to the Vinaya, and is properly settled:
it is performed for an offense; it is performed for an offense that is subject to confession; it is performed for an offense that has not been confessed … [as above] …”
It is done after having charged [the person]; it is done after having reminded [them]; it is done after having laid the offense upon [them] ...
[as before] ... it is done in the presence [of the accused]; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly ...
[as before] ... it is done after interrogation; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly ... [as before].
It is done with the admission [of the offense]; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done for an offense; it is done according to the Dhamma;
it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that requires confession; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe…
It has been performed regarding an offense that has not been confessed; it has been performed according to the Dhamma;
it has been performed by a unanimous assembly …pe… it has been performed after having charged [the person]; it has been performed according to the Dhamma;

it has been performed by a unanimous assembly …pe… it has been performed after having reminded [the person]; it has been performed according to the Dhamma; it has been performed by a unanimous assembly …pe…
When a formal act of reconciliation has been performed after charging someone with an offense, it is performed according to the Dhamma and it is performed by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a formal act of reconciliation possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and one that is well-settled.
The section on the twelvefold legitimate formal act of reconciliation is finished.
4.3. The Tetrad on Wishing “Monks, when a monk possesses five qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so wishes, may carry out a procedure of reconciliation against him:

he strives for the loss of householders; he strives for the harm of householders; he strives for the non-residence of householders; he reviles and insults householders; he causes division among householders.”
"Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may perform an act of reconciliation against a monk who possesses these five qualities.
Furthermore, monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may perform an act of reconciliation against a monk who possesses another five qualities:
he speaks dispraise of householders before the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma before householders, and he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha before householders..."
“He speaks dispraise; he reviles householders with what is base and ridicules them with what is base; he does not fulfill the righteous promise made to householders.
Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a procedure of reconciliation against a monk who possesses these five qualities.
Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a procedure of reconciliation against five kinds of monks.

One monk strives for the laypeople’s lack of gain; one strives for their harm; one strives for their non-residence; one reviles and insults the laypeople; and one causes dissension among the laypeople.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of reconciliation against these five monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of reconciliation against another five monks.
One speaks dispraise of the Buddha to householders; one speaks dispraise of the Dhamma to householders;
one speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha to householders; one reviles and insults householders with base things;
and one does not fulfill a righteous promise made to householders.
“Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out an act of reconciliation against these five monks.
The ‘Desire Tetrad’ is finished. 4.4.
The Eighteen Duties.”
“Monks, a monk against whom a *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* has been carried out must conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is proper conduct:
he must not confer full ordination;”
One should not grant dependence,
one should not have a novice attend upon oneself,
and one should not accept appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs.
Even when authorized, a monk must not exhort the bhikkhunīs.
He must not commit the same offense for which the Saṅgha has performed an act of reconciliation,
nor any other offense of a similar nature.
Or even worse than that:
the action is not to be censured,
nor is the agent to be censured.
The Uposatha should not be suspended for a regular monk;
the Pavāraṇā should not be suspended;
nor should he be made subject to commands.
One should not initiate a formal reprimand,
one should not grant an opportunity for defense,
and one should not issue a censure.
"He is not to be reminded [of his offense], nor is he to be associated with by the monks.
The eighteen duties regarding the act of reconciliation are concluded.
Then the Saṅgha performed an act of reconciliation against the bhikkhu Sudhamma, saying:
"The householder Citta must be asked for forgiveness by you.

to ask the householder Citta for forgiveness.

"Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has appointed the monk [name] as a messenger for the monk Sudhamma to ask the householder Citta for forgiveness.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this."
“Monks, that monk Sudhamma, together with a companion monk, should go to Macchikasaṇḍa and ask the householder Citta for forgiveness, saying:
‘Forgive me, householder; I seek your favor.
If he forgives when addressed in this way, that is good.”
If he does not forgive, the attendant monk should say:

If he forgives when thus addressed, that is good.

Then the Venerable Sudhamma, having gone to Macchikāsaṇḍa together with a messenger monk, asked the householder Citta for forgiveness.
He behaved properly, showed humility, and acted in a way that led to his release; he approached the monks and spoke thus:
"Friends, I have been subjected to a procedure of reconciliation by the Saṅgha, yet I am behaving properly, showing humility, and acting in a way that leads to my release."
“What course of action should I follow?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… “In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha rescind the act of reconciliation against the monk Sudhamma.”
4.5. The Group of Eighteen on Not to Be Revoked “Monks, the act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*) against a monk endowed with five factors is not to be revoked.

These are: he gives full ordination; he provides formal support (*nissaya*); he has a novice attend upon him; he consents to being appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he instructs the bhikkhunīs.”
Monks, the *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (act of reconciliation) against a monk endowed with these five factors should not be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, the *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* against a monk endowed with another five factors should not be lifted:
he commits the same offense for which the *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* was performed by the Saṅgha, or another of a similar nature, or one even more grave than that.
He blames the legal act; he blames those who carry out the legal act.
Monks, for a monk endowed with these five factors, a legal act of reconciliation should not be lifted.
Monks, for a monk endowed with eight factors, a legal act of reconciliation should not be lifted.
He cancels the Uposatha of a regular bhikkhu; he cancels the Pavāraṇā; he makes himself subject to being spoken to; he initiates a formal accusation; he demands an opportunity [to speak];

he reproaches him; he reminds him; he engages in disputes with other bhikkhus. Monks, when a bhikkhu possesses these eight factors, the legal procedure of reconciliation against him should not be lifted.
The group of eighteen on "the non-lifting of the legal procedure of reconciliation" is finished.
4.6. The Group of Eighteen on the Suspension of a Procedure “Monks, the procedure of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*) against a monk endowed with five factors should be suspended.

These are: he does not give the full admission (*upasampadā*); he does not provide formal support (*nissaya*); he does not have a novice attend upon him; he does not consent to being appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he does not instruct the bhikkhunīs.”
Monks, the procedure of reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīyakamma) should be lifted for a monk who possesses these five qualities.
Furthermore, monks, the procedure of reconciliation should be lifted for a monk who possesses another five qualities:
he does not commit the same offense for which the Saṅgha carried out the procedure of reconciliation against him, nor another of a similar nature, nor one more serious than that.
He does not criticize the legal act, nor does he criticize those who performed it—
for these five factors, monks, the *paṭisāraṇīya* legal act against a monk should be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, for a monk endowed with eight factors, the *paṭisāraṇīya* legal act should be lifted.

He does not cancel the Uposatha of a regular monk; he does not cancel the Pavāraṇā; he does not issue a command; he does not initiate a formal censure; he does not demand an opportunity for instruction; he does not accuse; he does not remind; he does not associate with other monks.
Monks, when a monk possesses these eight factors, the legal procedure of reconciliation against him should be suspended.
The group of eighteen on the suspension of the legal procedure of reconciliation is finished.
And furthermore, monks, it should be settled in this way:
That monk Sudhamma, monks, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder,
having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak to them thus:

‘Venerable sir, I have been subjected by the Saṅgha to the legal procedure of reconciliation; I am conducting myself properly, I am acting in accordance with the requirements, and I am living in a manner that leads to deliverance. I request the lifting of the legal procedure of reconciliation.
She should ask a second time;
she should ask a third time.
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.

This monk Sudhamma has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a procedure of reconciliation; he is conducting himself properly, he is acting in accordance with the Saṅgha’s wishes, he is behaving so as to deserve release, and he asks for the lifting of the procedure of reconciliation.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rescind the act of reconciliation against the bhikkhu Sudhamma.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.

This monk Sudhamma, against whom the Sangha has carried out a procedure of reconciliation, is conducting himself properly, he is acting in accordance with the requirements, he is behaving so as to reach the end of the matter, and he asks for the lifting of the procedure of reconciliation.
The Sangha lifts the procedure of reconciliation for the monk Sudhamma.
Whichever venerable one approves of the lifting of the procedure of reconciliation for the monk Sudhamma, let him be silent; [if not, let him speak].
Whoever does not approve of this, let him speak.
A second time I state this matter...
A third time I state this matter—
Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.

This monk Sudhamma, who has been subjected to a procedure of reconciliation by the Sangha, is conducting himself properly, he is compliant, he conducts himself in a way that leads to his release, and he requests the lifting of the procedure of reconciliation.
The Sangha lifts the procedure of reconciliation for the monk Sudhamma.
Whichever venerable one approves of the revocation of the act of reconciliation against the monk Sudhamma, let him be silent;
whichever does not approve, let him speak.
The Sangha has revoked the act of reconciliation against the monk Sudhamma.
“It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this.
The fourth section on the act of reconciliation is finished.
5. The Act of Suspension for Not Seeing an Offense.
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, the Venerable Channa, having committed an offense, did not wish to see that offense.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How indeed could the Venerable Channa, having committed an offense, not wish to see that offense?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that the monk Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to see that offense?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unbecoming...
How indeed, monks, could that foolish man, having fallen into an offense, not wish to see that offense?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on]...”
Having rebuked him … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha carry out a formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to recognize an offense.”
He shall not share in the community.
And this, monks, is how it should be done:

first, the monk Channa is to be accused; having been accused, he is to be reminded; having been reminded, the offense is to be charged against him; and having charged the offense, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
This bhikkhu Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to see that offense.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should carry out a formal act of suspension against the bhikkhu Channa for his refusal to see an offense.’
He shall have no communion with the Saṅgha.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
This bhikkhu Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to see that offense.
The Saṅgha is performing a formal act of suspension against the bhikkhu Channa for his refusal to see the offense—
a suspension from communion with the Saṅgha.
Whichever venerable one approves of performing the formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to recognize an offense— namely,
that he shall not share in communal life with the Saṅgha— let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak on this matter...
A third time I speak on this matter:
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
This bhikkhu Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to see that offense.
The Saṅgha is performing a formal act of suspension against the bhikkhu Channa for his refusal to see the offense—
a suspension from communion with the Saṅgha.
Whichever venerable one approves of performing the act of suspension against the monk Channa for his refusal to see an offense—
meaning non-association with the Saṅgha— let him be silent;
whoever does not approve should speak.
“The Saṅgha has performed a formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his refusal to see an offense—a suspension involving non-association with the Saṅgha.
This is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this.”
"And you should circulate the succession of dwellings, monks, thus:
'The monk Channa has been suspended by the Saṅgha for not seeing an offense;
he is not to have communion with the Saṅgha.'"

5.1. The Group of Twelve on Illegal Acts “Monks, when a procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense is endowed with three factors, it is an illegal act, a non-Discipline act, and one that is not properly settled.
It is performed in the absence of the accused; it is performed without having questioned [the accused]; it is performed without the admission [of the offense].”
“Monks, when it possesses these three factors, a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense is both a non-Dhamma act and a non-disciplinary act, and it is improperly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when it possesses another three factors, a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense is both a non-Dhamma act and a non-disciplinary act, and it is improperly settled:
it is done for one who has committed no offense; it is done for an offense that does not require confession; it is done for an offense that has already been confessed … [as before] …”
It is done without having charged [the person]; it is done without having reminded [them]; it is done without having laid an offense [upon them]...
it is done in their absence; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly...
it is done without questioning; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly...

It is done without the admission [of the offense]; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that is not an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma;
it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that does not require confession; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…
When an offense has been confessed, it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly ... [and so on] ...
it is done without having charged [the offender], it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly ... [and so on] ...
it is done without having reminded [the offender], it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly ... [and so on].
It is done without having charged him with an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, a procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense that possesses these three factors is a proceeding contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and improperly settled.
The group of twelve on procedures contrary to the Dhamma regarding the procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense is finished.

5.2. The Set of Twelve on Legal Acts Concerning Dhamma “Monks, when it possesses three factors, a legal act of suspension for not recognizing an offense is a legal act in accordance with the Dhamma, a legal act in accordance with the Vinaya, and is properly settled.
It is carried out in the presence [of the accused], it is carried out by questioning, and it is carried out upon admission.”
“Monks, when it possesses these three factors, a formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and is properly settled.
Furthermore, monks, when it possesses another three factors … [as before] … it is an offense that has been committed;
it is an offense that leads to confession; it is an offense that has not been confessed … [as before] …”
It has been done after having charged [the person]; it has been done after having reminded [them]; it has been done after having brought forward the offense ...
[and so on] ... it has been done in the presence [of the accused]; it has been done according to the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly ...
[and so on] ... it has been done after interrogation; it has been done according to the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly ... [and so on].

It is done with the admission [of the offense]; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done regarding an offense; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma;
it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done regarding an offense that requires confession; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe…
It has been done regarding an offense that has not been confessed; it has been done according to the Dhamma;
it has been done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it has been done after having charged [the person]; it has been done according to the Dhamma;
it has been done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it has been done after having reminded [the person]; it has been done according to the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly …pe…
It is done after having charged him with an offense; it is done in accordance with the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate legal act, a disciplinary legal act, and is properly settled.
The group of twelve on legitimate legal acts regarding the procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense is finished.
5.3. The Sixfold Set on Wishing “Monks, when a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so wishes, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his refusal to see an offense.
He is one who creates strife, creates quarrels, creates disputes, creates contention, and creates legal issues in the Saṅgha.”
He is foolish and incompetent, frequently committing offenses and failing to make amends for them;
he lives in association with householders through improper forms of association with householders.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his failure to recognize an offense.
“Monks, when a monk possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his failure to recognize an offense.
He has failed in higher virtue regarding virtue; he has failed in conduct regarding conduct; he has failed in view regarding views.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his failure to recognize an offense.”
“Furthermore, monks, if a monk possesses three other qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his failure to recognize an offense.
He speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
If a monk possesses these three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his failure to recognize an offense.”
“Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense against three kinds of monks:
one who is a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a maker of legal issues in the Saṅgha;
and one who is foolish, incompetent, abundant in offenses, and lacking in restraint.”
One who dwells in association with householders through improper forms of association with householders—
of these three kinds of monks, O bhikkhus, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense.
Furthermore, O bhikkhus, of another three kinds of monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense.
One has failed in virtue regarding higher morality; one has failed in conduct regarding improper behavior; one has failed in view regarding extreme views.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for failure to acknowledge an offense against these three kinds of monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for failure to acknowledge an offense against another three kinds of monks.
One speaks dispraise of the Buddha, one speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and one speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for non-recognition of an offense against these three monks.
The section on the six [cases] regarding the formal act of suspension for non-recognition of an offense is finished.
5.4. The Forty-Fourfold Conduct Monks, a monk against whom a formal act of suspension has been carried out for not seeing an offense should conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
One should not grant full ordination,
one should not give formal support,
and one should not have a novice attend upon oneself.
The appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs must not be accepted,
and even one who has been appointed must not instruct the bhikkhunīs. Furthermore,
that offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out an act of suspension for failure to recognize an offense must not be committed.
Whether it be other such [actions] or even worse than that,
one's deed should not be censured.
The officials are not to be censured.
There should be no salutation or rising up for a regular monk.
The act of joining the palms in salutation,
the act of respectful service,
and the offering of a seat.
The offering of a bed,
water for washing the feet, a footstool,
and a foot-washing stone.
The receiving of bowl and robes,
and the acceptance of back-massage while bathing,
may be permitted. A regular bhikkhu must not be accused of failure in virtue.
He should not be accused on account of failure in conduct,
nor should he be accused on account of failure in view,
nor should he be accused on account of failure in livelihood.
A bhikkhu should not cause schism among the bhikkhus;
he should not bear the banner of householders,
nor should he bear the banner of the sectarians.
One should not associate with those of other sects;
one should associate with bhikkhus and train in the training of bhikkhus.
A regular bhikkhu must not dwell under one roof with another bhikkhu who is not regular;
he must not dwell under one roof in a non-residence;
nor must he dwell under one roof, whether in a residence or a non-residence.
Upon seeing a regular bhikkhu, one should rise from one's seat;
a regular bhikkhu should not be treated with disrespect, whether inside or outside.
One should not cancel the Uposatha of a regular bhikkhu.
The invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) must not be suspended;
one must not issue a command,
nor should an accusation be brought forward.
One should not grant him leave,
one should not accuse him,
and one should not remind him.
"He should not associate with the monks.
The forty-three points of conduct regarding the formal act of suspension for failure to recognize an offense are finished.
Then the Saṅgha performed a formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for failure to recognize an offense.
He was not to share in the community.
Having been subjected by the community to a formal act of suspension for failure to recognize an offense, he went from that residence to another residence.

There, the monks neither saluted him, nor rose up for him, nor performed the añjali-greeting, nor the duties of proper conduct; they did not honor him, did not revere him, did not esteem him, and did not worship him.
Thus, being neither honored, nor revered, nor esteemed, nor worshipped, and being treated with disrespect by the bhikkhus, he went from that residence to another residence.

There too, the bhikkhus did not salute him, nor rise for him, nor perform the añjali-greeting, nor perform the duties of respect; they did not honor him, nor revere him, nor esteem him, nor worship him.
Being neither honored, nor revered, nor esteemed, nor worshipped, and being treated with disrespect by the bhikkhus, he went from that residence as well to yet another residence.

There too, the monks neither saluted him, nor rose for him, nor performed the añjali-greeting, nor the proper duties of respect; they did not honor him, did not revere him, did not esteem him, and did not worship him.
Being thus unhonored, unrevered, unesteemed, and unworshipped by the monks, and being treated with disrespect, he returned once again to Kosambī.
There he conducted himself properly, behaved with humility, and acted in a way that was not conducive to his departure; he approached the monks and spoke to them thus:

“Friends, I have been subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense. I am conducting myself properly, I am acting in accordance with the rules, and I am conducting myself so as to deserve release. How, then, should I proceed? The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One… [as before]… The Blessed One said: “Monks, let the Saṅgha grant that monk, who has been subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense, the act of reconciliation. And thus, monks, it should be done: First, that monk should be made to confess his offense. Then, having approached the Saṅgha, he should arrange his robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior monks, squat on his heels, raise his joined palms, and say: “Venerable sirs, I, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense, have now confessed my offense. May the Saṅgha grant me the act of reconciliation. This should be stated three times. Then a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk so-and-so, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense, has confessed his offense. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant him the act of reconciliation. This is the motion. ‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk so-and-so, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense, has confessed his offense. The Saṅgha grants him the act of reconciliation. Let any venerable one who approves of granting the act of reconciliation to the monk so-and-so, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense, remain silent; any who do not approve should speak. For the second time I speak forth this matter: Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me… [repeat as above]… For the third time I speak forth this matter: Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me… [repeat as above]… The Saṅgha grants the act of reconciliation to the monk so-and-so, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.’”
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha rescind the act of suspension against the monk Channa for his refusal to see an offense.
5.5. The Group of Forty-three on What Should Not Be Rescinded:
“Monks, when a monk possesses five qualities, the act of suspension for his refusal to see an offense should not be rescinded.”
He gives full ordination; he gives formal support; he has a novice attend upon him; he accepts appointment as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he exhorts the bhikkhunīs.
Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses these five qualities, on account of his failure to see an offense, is not to be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses another five qualities, on account of his failure to see an offense, is not to be lifted.
If a monk commits that very offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out an act of suspension for non-seeing of an offense, or another offense similar to it, or one more serious than it;
if he criticizes the legal procedure and criticizes those who performed the procedure—
for these five factors, monks, the act of suspension for non-seeing of an offense should not be lifted for a monk.
“Monks, for a monk who possesses another five qualities, the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense shall not be lifted.
He accepts the bowing down, the rising up, the salutation with joined palms, the proper homage, and the offering of a seat from a regular monk.
Monks, for a monk who possesses these five qualities, the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense shall not be lifted.”
“Monks, for a monk who possesses another five qualities, the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense should not be lifted.
He consents to a regular monk’s being offered a bed, water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-scraper, the receiving of his bowl and robe, and back-massage during bathing.
Monks, for a monk who possesses these five qualities, the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense should not be lifted.”
“Monks, for another five qualities, the act of suspension for a monk’s failure to recognize an offense should not be lifted.

He slanders a regular monk with failure in virtue; he slanders him with failure in conduct; he slanders him with failure in view; he slanders him with failure in livelihood; he causes division among monks.”
Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses these five factors, on account of his failure to recognize an offense, must not be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses another five factors, on account of his failure to recognize an offense, must not be lifted:
he wears the banner of a householder, he wears the banner of a sectarian, and he associates with sectarians.
"He does not associate with the bhikkhus;
he does not train in the training of the bhikkhus"—endowed with these five factors, monks, the procedure of suspension for a bhikkhu who does not see an offense is not to be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, endowed with another five factors, the procedure of suspension for a bhikkhu who does not see an offense is not to be lifted.

He lives in a covered dwelling together with a regular bhikkhu; he lives in a covered non-dwelling together with a regular bhikkhu; he lives in either a covered dwelling or a covered non-dwelling together with a regular bhikkhu;
upon seeing a regular bhikkhu, he does not rise from his seat;
or he encroaches upon a regular bhikkhu, whether inside or outside [the dwelling].
Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses these five factors, on account of his failure to recognize an offense, must not be lifted.
Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses eight factors, on account of his failure to recognize an offense, must not be lifted:

he cancels the Uposatha of a regular monk; he cancels the Pavāraṇā; he issues a command; he initiates a formal accusation; he demands an opportunity to speak; he reproves; he reminds; he involves himself in disputes with other monks.
Monks, for a monk endowed with these eight factors, the formal act of suspension for failure to recognize an offense is not to be lifted.
The section of forty-three cases on when the formal act of suspension for failure to recognize an offense is not to be lifted is finished.
5.6. The Section of Forty-three Cases on When it Is to Be Lifted.
“Monks, the legal procedure of suspension for a monk who does not acknowledge an offense should be lifted when he possesses five qualities:

he does not give full ordination; he does not provide formal support; he does not have a novice attend upon him; he does not accept appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he does not instruct the bhikkhunīs.
Monks, the legal procedure of suspension for a monk who does not acknowledge an offense should be lifted when he possesses these five qualities.”
“Monks, a procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense should also be lifted for a monk who possesses five other qualities:
he does not commit the same offense for which the Sangha carried out the procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense, nor another similar one, nor one worse than that;
he does not criticize the legal act, nor does he criticize those who performed it.”
Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who fails to recognize an offense should be lifted when he possesses these five qualities.
Furthermore, monks, the act of suspension for a monk who fails to recognize an offense should be lifted when he possesses another five qualities:
he does not accept the formal salutation, rising to greet, joining of palms, respectful service, or the offering of a seat from a regular monk.
Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses these five qualities, on account of his failure to recognize an offense, should be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses another five qualities, on account of his failure to recognize an offense, should be lifted:

he does not accept the offering of a bed from a regular monk, nor water for washing the feet, nor a footstool, nor a foot-scraper, nor the receiving of bowl and robe, nor the rubbing of the back during bathing.
Monks, the procedure of suspension for a monk who does not recognize an offense should be lifted when he possesses these five qualities.
Furthermore, monks, the procedure of suspension for a monk who does not recognize an offense should also be lifted when he possesses another five qualities.
He does not accuse a regular bhikkhu of failure in virtue, he does not accuse him of failure in conduct, he does not accuse him of failure in view, he does not accuse him of failure in livelihood,
and he does not cause a bhikkhu to be split from other bhikkhus— it is for these five factors, monks, that the act of suspension for a bhikkhu who has not seen his offense should be lifted.
“Monks, for a monk who possesses five other qualities, the procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense should be lifted.
He does not wear the insignia of a householder; he does not wear the insignia of a sectarian; he does not associate with sectarians; he associates with monks; and he trains in the training of a monk.
Monks, for a monk who possesses these five qualities, the procedure of suspension for not seeing an offense should be lifted.”
“Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who has not acknowledged an offense should also be lifted when he possesses another five qualities:
he does not live under the same roof as a regular monk in a monastery; he does not live under the same roof as a regular monk in a non-monastery;
he does not live under the same roof as a regular monk in either a monastery or a non-monastery; and upon seeing a regular monk, he rises from his seat.”
He does not harass a regular bhikkhu, whether inside or outside [the monastery].
It is, monks, when a bhikkhu possesses these five factors that the act of suspension for failure to recognize an offense should be lifted.
Monks, it is when a bhikkhu possesses eight factors that the act of suspension for failure to recognize an offense should be lifted.

He does not suspend the Uposatha of a regular monk; he does not suspend the Pavāraṇā; he does not issue a command; he does not initiate a formal censure; he does not demand an opportunity [to speak]; he does not accuse; he does not remind; he does not associate with other monks.
Monks, when a monk possesses these eight factors, the procedure of suspension for failure to recognize an offense should be lifted.
The group of forty-three cases concerning the lifting of the procedure of suspension for failure to recognize an offense is finished.
And furthermore, monks, it should be settled in this way.

That monk Channa, monks, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, I, who have been subjected by the Saṅgha to an act of suspension for not seeing an offense, am conducting myself properly; my hair...”
‘I submit myself; I declare my rehabilitation; I request the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense.
She should request this a second time, and she should request it a third time.
A competent monk who has mastered the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk Channa, having been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense, is now conducting himself properly.”
He has shaved his hair; he is fit to be released; he requests the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha lift the formal act of suspension for Channa the bhikkhu for not seeing an offense.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk Channa has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense;

he is conducting himself properly, he is acting in accordance with the Dhamma, he is behaving so as to deserve release, and he requests the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense."
The Sangha rescinds the act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to recognize an offense.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the rescinding of the act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to recognize an offense, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
A third time I speak this matter:
Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This monk Channa has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense;
he is conducting himself properly, he is acting in accordance with the Dhamma, he is striving for deliverance, and he requests the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense.
The Saṅgha lifts the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense against the monk Channa.
Whichever venerable one approves of the lifting of the formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to recognize an offense, let him be silent;
whichever does not approve, let him speak.
The formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to recognize an offense has been lifted by the Saṅgha.
“It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this.
The fifth section, on the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, is concluded.
6. The Act of Suspension for Not Making Amends for an Offense.
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Channa, having committed an offense, did not wish to make amends for that offense.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged him, and complained, saying:
“How indeed could the Venerable Channa, having fallen into an offense, not wish to make amends for that offense?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that the monk Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to make amends for that offense?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is improper, monks...
How indeed, monks, could that foolish man, having committed an offense, not wish to make amends for that offense?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so forth].”
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha carry out a formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to make amends for an offense.”
He shall not share in the community.
And this, monks, is how it should be done:

first, the monk Channa is to be accused; having been accused, he is to be reminded; having been reminded, the offense is to be charged; and having had the offense charged, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
This monk Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to make amends for that offense.
If it seems appropriate to the Sangha, the Sangha should carry out a formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to make amends for an offense.’
He shall have no communion with the Saṅgha.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
This monk Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to make amends for that offense.
The Saṅgha is performing an act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to make amends for an offense—
a suspension from communion with the Saṅgha.
Whichever venerable one approves of performing the formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to make amends for an offense—
meaning non-association with the Saṅgha— let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
A third time I speak this matter:
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This bhikkhu Channa, having committed an offense, does not wish to make amends for that offense.
The Saṅgha is performing a formal act of suspension against the bhikkhu Channa for his failure to make amends for an offense— namely,
non-participation in communal affairs with the Saṅgha.
Whichever venerable one approves of performing the act of suspension for the monk Channa on account of his failure to make amends for an offense—
including exclusion from communal life with the Saṅgha— let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The Saṅgha has carried out a formal act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to make amends for an offense—a suspension involving non-association with the Saṅgha.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this.”
"And you should circulate the succession of dwellings, monks, thus:
'The monk Channa has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a procedure of suspension for not making amends for an offense—
he is not to have communion with the Saṅgha.'"

6.1. The Group of Twelve on Invalid Legal Acts “Monks, when a legal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense is endowed with three factors, it is an invalid legal act, a non-disciplinary legal act, and one that is not properly settled.
It is done in the absence of the accused; it is done without having questioned [the accused]; it is done without the consent [of the accused].”
“Monks, when a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense is endowed with these three factors, it is an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled.

Furthermore, monks, when a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense is endowed with another three factors, it is an illegitimate act, contrary to the discipline, and improperly settled:

it is performed against one who has committed no offense; it is performed against one who has committed an offense that does not require confession; it is performed against one who has already confessed the offense... [and so on].”
It is done without having charged [the person]; it is done without having reminded [them]; it is done without having laid an offense [upon them]...
[as above] ...it is done in their absence; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly...
[as above] ...it is done without interrogation; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly... [as above] ...
It is done without the consent [of the accused]; it is done contrary to the Dhamma;
it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that is not an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma;
it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that does not require confession; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…
When an offense has been confessed, it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done without having charged [the offender],

it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe… it is done without having reminded [the offender], it is done contrary to the Dhamma, it is done by an incomplete assembly …pe…
It is done without having charged him with an offense; it is done contrary to the Dhamma; it is done by an incomplete assembly.
Monks, when a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense possesses these three factors, it is an illegitimate legal act, it is contrary to the Vinaya, and it is improperly settled.
The group of twelve on illegitimate legal acts regarding suspension for not making amends for an offense is finished.

6.2. The Set of Twelve on Legal Acts Concerning Dhamma “Monks, when a legal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense possesses three factors, it is a legal act in accordance with the Dhamma, a legal act in accordance with the Vinaya, and is properly settled.
It is performed in the presence [of the accused], it is performed after interrogation, and it is performed with the admission [of the offense].”
“Monks, when it possesses these three factors, a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and one that is well-settled.

Furthermore, monks, when it possesses another three factors, a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and one that is well-settled:
it is done for an offense; it is done for an offense that is subject to confession; it is done for an offense that has not been confessed … [as above] …”
It has been done after having accused; it has been done after having reminded; it has been done after having charged with an offense ...
[as above] ... it has been done in the presence of; it has been done according to the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly ...
[as above] ... it has been done after interrogation; it has been done according to the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly ... [as above] ...
It is done with the admission [of the offense]; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done for an offense; it is done according to the Dhamma;
it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it is done for an offense that requires confession; it is done according to the Dhamma; it is done by a unanimous assembly …pe…
It has been done regarding an offense that has not been confessed; it has been done in accordance with the Dhamma;
it has been done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it has been done after having charged [the person]; it has been done in accordance with the Dhamma;
it has been done by a unanimous assembly …pe… it has been done after having reminded [the person]; it has been done in accordance with the Dhamma; it has been done by a unanimous assembly …pe…

When a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense has been carried out after the offense has been formally charged, it is done in accordance with the Dhamma and by a unanimous assembly.
Monks, when a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense possesses these three factors, it is a legitimate act, a disciplinary act, and well-settled.
The group of twelve on legitimate acts of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense is finished.

6.3. The Sixfold Set on Wishing “Monks, when a monk possesses three qualities, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension against him for his failure to make amends for an offense.
He is a maker of strife, a maker of quarrels, a maker of disputes, a maker of contention, and a creator of legal issues within the Saṅgha.”
He is foolish, incompetent, frequently committing offenses, and has not made amends for them;
he dwells in association with householders through improper forms of association with householders.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension against him for his failure to make amends for an offense.
“Monks, when a monk possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for non-atonement of an offense against him.
He has failed in higher virtue, he has failed in conduct, and he has failed in view.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for non-atonement of an offense against him.”
“Monks, when a monk possesses another three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his failure to make amends for an offense.
He speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
Monks, when a monk possesses these three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for his failure to make amends for an offense.”
“Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for non-atonement of an offense against three kinds of monks:
one who is a creator of quarrels, a creator of strife, a creator of disputes, a creator of contention, and a creator of legal issues in the Saṅgha;
and one who is foolish, incompetent, prone to offenses, and lacking in discernment.”
One who dwells in association with householders in ways that are improper for such association—
of these three kinds of monks, O bhikkhus, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of suspension for non-atonement of an offense.
Furthermore, O bhikkhus, of another three kinds of monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of suspension for non-atonement of an offense.
One has failed in virtue regarding higher virtue; one has failed in conduct regarding conduct; one has failed in view regarding views.
Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for non-atonement of an offense against these three kinds of monks.
Furthermore, monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may carry out a formal act of suspension for non-atonement of an offense against another three kinds of monks.
One speaks dispraise of the Buddha, one speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, and one speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha.
Monks, if the Saṅgha so desires, it may carry out a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense against these three monks.
The section on the six [cases] regarding the formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense is finished.
6.4. The Forty-Fourfold Conduct Monks, a monk against whom a formal act of suspension has been carried out for failure to make amends for an offense should conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
One should not confer full ordination,
one should not grant formal dependence,
and one should not have a novice attend upon oneself.
The appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs must not be accepted,
nor should one who has been appointed instruct the bhikkhunīs. Furthermore,
one must not commit that same offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends.
Whether it be another of a similar kind or even more blameworthy than that,
one's action should not be censured.
The officials are not to be censured.
One should not perform salutation or rising up for a regular monk.
the act of joining the palms in salutation,
the act of respectful service,
and the offering of a seat.
The offering of a bed,
water for the feet, a footstool,
and a foot-washing stone.
The receiving of bowl and robes,
and the acceptance of back-massage during bathing,
may be permitted. A regular bhikkhu must not be accused of failure in virtue.
He should not be accused on account of a failure in conduct,
nor should he be accused on account of a failure in view,
nor should he be accused on account of a failure in livelihood.
A bhikkhu must not be divided from other bhikkhus.
One must not bear the banner of householders,
nor must one bear the banner of the sectarians.
One should not associate with those of other sects;
one should associate with monks and train in the training of monks.
A regular monk must not dwell under one roof with another regular monk in a residence;
he must not dwell under one roof with another regular monk in a non-residence;
nor must he dwell under one roof with another regular monk, whether in a residence or a non-residence.
Upon seeing a regular bhikkhu, one should rise from one's seat;
a regular bhikkhu should not be obstructed, whether inside or outside.
One should not cancel the Uposatha of a regular bhikkhu.
The invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) must not be suspended;
one must not issue a command,
nor should an accusation be brought forward.
An opportunity should not be granted;
one should not be accused;
one should not be reminded.
"He should not associate with the bhikkhus.
The forty-three duties regarding the formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense are concluded.
Then the Saṅgha performed a formal act of suspension against the bhikkhu Channa for failure to make amends for an offense.
He was not to share in the community.
Having been subjected by the community to a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense, he went from that residence to another residence.
There, the monks neither saluted him, nor rose up for him, nor performed the añjali-gesture, nor paid him proper respect; they did not honor him, revere him, esteem him, or worship him.
Thus, being neither honored, nor respected, nor esteemed, nor revered, and being treated with disrespect by the bhikkhus, he went from that residence to another residence.
There too, the bhikkhus did not salute him, nor rise for him, nor perform the añjali-greeting, nor the duties of hospitality; they did not honor him, respect him, esteem him, or revere him.
Being neither honored, nor respected, nor esteemed, nor revered, and being treated with disrespect by the bhikkhus, he went from that residence as well to yet another residence.
There too, the bhikkhus neither saluted him, nor rose for him, nor performed the añjali-greeting, nor paid him proper homage; they did not honor him, revere him, esteem him, or worship him.
Being thus unhonored, unrevered, unesteemed, and unworshipped by the bhikkhus, and being treated with disrespect, he returned once more to Kosambī.
There he conducted himself properly, showed humility, and behaved in a way that deserved to be excused; then, approaching the bhikkhus, he spoke thus:

“Friends, I have been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense. I am conducting myself properly, I am acting in accordance with the rules, and I am striving for deliverance. How, then, should I proceed? The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One… [as before]… The Blessed One said: “Monks, if a monk who has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense conducts himself properly, acts in accordance with the rules, and strives for deliverance, he should approach the Saṅgha and say: ‘Venerable sirs, I, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense, am conducting myself properly, I am acting in accordance with the rules, and I am striving for deliverance. May the Saṅgha grant me the lifting of that formal act of suspension. A second time, monks, he should approach the Saṅgha and say: ‘Venerable sirs, I, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense, am conducting myself properly, I am acting in accordance with the rules, and I am striving for deliverance. May the Saṅgha grant me the lifting of that formal act of suspension. A third time, monks, he should approach the Saṅgha and say: ‘Venerable sirs, I, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense, am conducting myself properly, I am acting in accordance with the rules, and I am striving for deliverance. May the Saṅgha grant me the lifting of that formal act of suspension. Then, monks, four or five monks should lift that formal act of suspension. One of them should announce: ‘May the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. This monk so-and-so, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense, is conducting himself properly, is acting in accordance with the rules, and is striving for deliverance. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should lift the formal act of suspension for so-and-so. This is the motion. ‘May the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. This monk so-and-so, who was subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense, is conducting himself properly, is acting in accordance with the rules, and is striving for deliverance. The Saṅgha lifts the formal act of suspension for so-and-so. Whoever among the venerable ones approves of lifting the formal act of suspension for so-and-so, let him remain silent; whoever does not approve, let him speak. For the second time, I speak forth this matter: may the venerable Saṅgha listen to me… For the third time, I speak forth this matter: may the venerable Saṅgha listen to me… The Saṅgha lifts the formal act of suspension for so-and-so. It is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.’”
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha rescind the act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to make amends for an offense.
6.5. The Set of Forty-three on What Should Not Be Rescinded “Monks, when a monk possesses five qualities, the act of suspension for his failure to make amends for an offense shall not be rescinded.”
“He gives full ordination; he gives formal support; he has a novice attend him; he accepts appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he instructs bhikkhunīs.
Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses these five factors, for not making amends for an offense, is not to be lifted.
Furthermore, monks, the act of suspension for a monk who possesses another five factors, for not making amends for an offense, is not to be lifted.”
He commits that very offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out a procedure of suspension for non-atonement, or another offense similar to it, or one more blameworthy than that;
he criticizes the legal act and criticizes those who performed the act … [and so on] … he accepts the salutation,
the rising up, the joining of palms, the formal courtesy, and the offering of a seat from a regular monk … [and so on] …
He consents to a regular bhikkhu’s being offered a bed, water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing stone, the receiving of his bowl and robe, and back-massage while bathing.

… He slanders a regular bhikkhu with a failure in virtue, he slanders him with a failure in conduct, he slanders him with a failure in view, he slanders him with a failure in livelihood; he causes a bhikkhu to be split from other bhikkhus. … [and so on] …”
He wears the banner of a householder; he wears the banner of a sectarian; he associates with sectarians; he does not associate with monks; he does not train in the training of a monk...
[and so on] ...he dwells under one roof in a residence together with a regular monk; he dwells under one roof in a non-residence;
he dwells under one roof in either a residence or a non-residence; having seen a regular monk, he does not rise from his seat.
He harasses a regular bhikkhu, whether inside or outside [the monastery].
Endowed with these five factors, monks, the act of suspension for a bhikkhu who has not made amends for an offense is not to be lifted.
Monks, endowed with eight factors, the act of suspension for a bhikkhu who has not made amends for an offense is not to be lifted.
If a monk suspends the Uposatha of a regular monk, suspends the Pavāraṇā, issues a command, initiates a formal accusation, demands an opportunity for defense,

accuses him, reminds him of an offense, or engages in disputes with other monks— monks, it is when a monk possesses these eight factors that a procedure of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense shall not be lifted.
The group of forty-three cases on the non-lifting of the procedure of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense is finished.

6.6. The Group of Forty-three on the Suspension of a Formal Act “Monks, when a monk possesses five factors, the formal act of suspension for his failure to make amends for an offense should be suspended.

These are: he does not ordain; he does not grant dependence; he does not have a novice attend upon him; he does not accept appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he does not instruct the bhikkhunīs.”
“Monks, the act of suspension for a monk who has not made amends for an offense should be lifted when he possesses these five qualities.
Furthermore, monks, the act of suspension for a monk who has not made amends for an offense should be lifted when he possesses another five qualities:
he does not commit that same offense for which the Sangha carried out the act of suspension for not making amends, nor does he commit another of a similar nature, nor one worse than that.”
He does not criticize the action, nor does he criticize the one who performed the action...
[and so on] ...he does not accept from a regular monk (pakatatta) a salutation, rising up, joining of palms, respectful gesture, or the offering of a seat...

[and so on] ...he does not accept from a regular monk the offering of a bed, water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing stone, the receiving of his bowl and robe, or the rubbing of his back while bathing... [and so on] ...

He does not accuse a regular bhikkhu of failure in virtue, nor of failure in conduct, nor of failure in view, nor of failure in livelihood; he does not cause a bhikkhu to be split from other bhikkhus...

[and so on] ...he does not wear the insignia of a householder, nor the insignia of a monastic wanderer; he does not associate with monastic wanderers, but associates with bhikkhus and trains in the training of bhikkhus... [and so on].
He does not dwell under one roof with a regular bhikkhu in a residence; he does not dwell under one roof with a regular bhikkhu in a non-residence;
he does not dwell under one roof with a regular bhikkhu in either a residence or a non-residence. Upon seeing a regular bhikkhu, he rises from his seat;
he does not encroach upon a regular bhikkhu, whether inside or outside.
Monks, for a monk who possesses these five factors, the formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense should be lifted.
Monks, for a monk who possesses eight factors, the formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense should be lifted.

He does not cancel the Uposatha of a regular monk; he does not cancel the Pavāraṇā; he does not issue a command; he does not initiate a formal accusation; he does not demand an opportunity [to speak]; he does not reprove; he does not remind; he does not associate with other monks.
Monks, when a monk possesses these eight factors, the legal procedure of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense should be lifted.
The group of forty-three cases on the lifting of the legal procedure of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense is finished.
And furthermore, monks, it should be settled in this way.

That monk Channa, monks, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the elder monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, I, who have been subjected by the Saṅgha to the act of suspension for not making amends for an offense, am conducting myself properly.”
‘I cast off my hair; I declare myself cleared of the offense; I request the lifting of the formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense.
He should request this a second time and a third time.
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk Channa has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for failure to make amends for an offense; he is now conducting himself properly.”
He has shaved his hair; he is fit for release; he requests the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha lift the formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense against the monk Channa.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This bhikkhu Channa has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense;
he now conducts himself properly, behaves with humility, and acts toward his rehabilitation. He requests the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense."
The Saṅgha rescinds the act of suspension for the monk Channa on account of his failure to make amends for an offense.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the rescinding of the act of suspension for the monk Channa on account of his failure to make amends for an offense, let him remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
A third time I speak this matter:
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This bhikkhu Channa has been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of suspension for not making amends for an offense.

He is conducting himself properly, he lowers his hair (in humility), he conducts himself so as to deserve release, and he requests the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not making amends for the offense.
The Saṅgha lifts the formal act of suspension for not making amends for the offense against the bhikkhu Channa.
Whichever venerable one approves of the lifting of the act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to atone for an offense, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Sangha has lifted the act of suspension against the monk Channa for his failure to atone for an offense.
“It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
The sixth chapter on the act of suspension for not making amends for an offense is finished.
7. The act of suspension for not relinquishing an evil view.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a pernicious view had arisen in a monk named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, as follows:
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.”
A number of bhikkhus heard that a pernicious view had arisen in the bhikkhu named Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, to the effect:
"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
Then those bhikkhus went to where the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, was staying.
Having approached the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, who had formerly been a vulture-keeper, they said this to him:
"Is it true, friend Ariṭṭha, that such an evil view has arisen in you:
'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called "obstructive states" by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them'?"

“Friend, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
“Do not say so, friend Ariṭṭha!
Do not misrepresent the Blessed One!”
"It is not right to misrepresent the Blessed One;
the Blessed One would not speak in such a way.
For in many ways, friend Ariṭṭha, the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstructions."
Moreover, for one who indulges in them, they will lead to obstacles.
"Sensual pleasures have been called 'of little satisfaction' by the Blessed One; they are full of suffering, full of despair; the danger in them is greater.
"Sensual pleasures have been compared to a skeleton by the Blessed One; they are full of suffering, full of despair; the danger in them is greater."

“Sensual pleasures have been compared to a lump of meat by the Blessed One … [as above] … sensual pleasures have been compared to a torch of grass by the Blessed One … [as above] … sensual pleasures have been compared to a pit of glowing coals by the Blessed One …”
The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a dream;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods;
the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree.
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a razor’s edge;
